findings.description: Dynamic import via import_module in pydantic __getattr__ lazy-loading module map
findings.reasoning: The module path passed to import_module comes from a module-level constant dict (`_dynamic_imports = {'RootModel': '.root_model'}`), keyed by an attribute name that must be present as a key in that dict. The attribute name is never interpolated into the import path, so an attacker cannot influence which module is imported. This is pydantic's standard PEP 562 lazy import pattern; there is no untrusted-data flow into the sink.

evidence.code_context: _dynamic_imports = {'RootModel': '.root_model'}; module = import_module(_dynamic_imports[attr_name], package=__package__)
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Sink argument is a constant value read from a hardcoded dict; the only variable part (attr_name) is used purely as a dict key and must already exist in the dict, otherwise _getattr_migration is called.
evidence.notes: No user-controlled input reaches the module path. Standard lazy-import idiom.

findings.description: ImportString validator performs arbitrary module import/attribute lookup on user-supplied dotted path
findings.reasoning: `import_string` is wired as the pydantic validator for the public `ImportString` annotation (pydantic/types.py:461) and for `_migration` lookups. When a model field is typed `ImportString[Any]`, a plain string taken directly from the validated input (e.g. JSON body) is split and passed to `importlib.import_module`, then `getattr`. An attacker controlling that field can therefore force the application to import any already-installed module and obtain any attribute from it (e.g. `os:system`, `subprocess:Popen`), which the application may later invoke. This is documented/intended behaviour of ImportString (opt-in by the developer), and it only reaches modules already importable, so it is not directly RCE in the library itself — but it is a genuine attacker-controlled dynamic-import primitive whose security depends entirely on how the consuming application uses the resolved attribute. Flagged for manual review of downstream usage rather than an outright library vulnerability.

evidence.code_context: pydantic/types.py:461: function=_validators.import_string — ImportString annotation uses this as validator. _validators.py:58-100 splits dotted_path on ':' and calls importlib.import_module(module_path) then getattr(module, attribute).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: validated model input string -> import_string(value) -> _import_string_logic -> import_module(module_path). No allow-list / no restriction on module names; only ImportError handling.
evidence.notes: Reachable also from pydantic/_migration.py:277-287 but there the paths are looked up from constant MOVED_IN_V2/REDIRECT_TO_V1 dicts. Tests (tests/test_types.py:1000) confirm arbitrary strings are passed through validation.

findings.description: pickle.loads in v1 parse helper — guarded by explicit allow_pickle flag (default False)
findings.reasoning: pickle.loads is only reached when the caller explicitly passes allow_pickle=True (or a content_type ending in 'pickle' together with allow_pickle=True). With the default allow_pickle=False the code raises RuntimeError before deserialization. Note that load_file selecting proto=pickle for '.pkl' suffix still hits the RuntimeError guard unless the caller opted in. This is the documented, opt-in escape hatch; the library cannot deserialize pickles from untrusted data unless the developer explicitly enables it, so the sink is an intentional, guarded feature rather than a vulnerability in this package.

findings.description: v1 import_string performs arbitrary module import/attribute lookup on user-supplied path (PyObject/ImportString validators)
findings.reasoning: v1's `import_string` is invoked by the `PyObject` field type validator (pydantic/v1/types.py:657: `return import_string(value)`), which converts a plain string from validated input into an imported attribute. A model field typed `PyObject` (or `ImportString`) therefore lets whoever controls the input select an arbitrary dotted path; the application receives the corresponding module attribute (e.g. a callable). This is a documented v1 feature and not exploitable in the library on its own, but it is an attacker-influenced dynamic-import primitive limited only by what is importable in the process. Manual review needed to confirm downstream consumers don't invoke the returned object.

findings.description: ReDoS (CVE-2024-3772) in pydantic v2 pretty-email regex: nested quantifier on attacker-controlled EmailStr input causes catastrophic/quadratic backtracking in `pretty_email_regex.fullmatch(value)`
findings.code_snippet:
def _build_pretty_email_regex() -> re.Pattern:
    name_chars = r'[\w!#$%&\'*+\-/=?^_`{|}~]'
    unquoted_name_group = fr'((?:{name_chars}+\s+)*{name_chars}+)'
    quoted_name_group = r'"((?:[^"]|\")+)"'
    email_group = r'<\s*(.+)\s*>'
    return re.compile(rf'\s*(?:{unquoted_name_group}|{quoted_name_group})?\s*{email_group}\s*')


pretty_email_regex = _build_pretty_email_regex()
findings.reasoning:
The regex built at pydantic/networks.py:389-397 contains a nested quantifier: `((?:[\w!#$%&'*+\-/=?^_`{|}~]+\s+)*[\w!#$%&'*+\-/=?^_`{|}~]+)`, where the inner `+` is wrapped by the outer `*` over a group that can match overlapping characters (`\s` is also accepted by the char class because of `\w` semantics? no — but the group `(?:name_chars+\s+)*` followed by `name_chars+` allows many ways to partition the same input because `\s` characters can be consumed by the outer repetition and re-matched by the trailing `name_chars+` due to the trailing `\s*` overlap). Concretely, a long run of word/space characters followed by an unterminated/absent `<...>` part makes the engine explore exponentially/many partitions before failing, i.e. catastrophic backtracking.

The regex is applied directly to untrusted user input in validate_email() at line 413: `m = pretty_email_regex.fullmatch(value)`, which is the validator behind `EmailStr` (pydantic/networks.py EmailStr / `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` -> plain validator -> validate_email). Any application validating an email field (login/registration endpoints, form input, API payloads) passes attacker-controlled strings into this regex at import-loaded, module-level compiled pattern.

This is exactly CVE-2024-3772 (pydantic < 2.4.0, fixed in 2.4.0 by rewriting pretty_email_regex). The package version here is 2.3.0 (pydantic/version.py: VERSION = '2.3.0'), so it is unpatched. Impact: a single request with a ~few-KB crafted email string pins a CPU core for seconds/minutes -> application-wide denial of service (CWE-1333 / CWE-400).

findings.description: Nested-quantifier regex in JsonSchema defs-ref normalization is applied only to internally generated core_ref strings, not attacker-controlled input
findings.code_snippet: components = [re.sub(r'(?:[^.[\]]+\.)+((?:[^.[\]]+))', r'\1', x) for x in components]
findings.reasoning: The regex flagged in `GenerateJsonSchema.get_defs_ref` operates on `core_ref`, which is a pydantic-core reference string synthesized during JSON schema generation (e.g. `__main__.Model:12345-foo.Field:6789`). It is derived from class/code metadata at schema-build time, not from request/user data. An attacker cannot inject an arbitrary `core_ref` into this call without already executing code. Additionally, `[^.[\]]+\.)+((?:[^.[\]]+))` is not catastrophically backtracking in practice: the inner class excludes `.` and `]`, so each iteration consumes at least one char with a deterministic separator; the nesting is over a disjoint alphabet, so there is no exponential ambiguity. Also, pydantic 2.3.0's real ReDoS issue (CVE-2024-3772) is in `pydantic/networks.py`'s pretty email regex, already reported separately.

evidence.code_context:
def get_defs_ref(self, core_mode_ref: CoreModeRef) -> DefsRef:
    core_ref, mode = core_mode_ref
    components = re.split(r'([\][,])', core_ref)
    components = [x.split(':')[0] for x in components]
    core_ref_no_id = ''.join(components)
    components = [re.sub(r'(?:[^.[\]]+\.)+((?:[^.[\]]+))', r'\1', x) for x in components]
evidence.dataflow_analysis: No path found from any HTTP/user input source to `core_ref`; `get_defs_ref` is invoked by the schema generator over `CoreRef`s built from model field annotations at schema build/'cache' time. grep_search for pretty_email_regex confirms which regexes handle user input (networks.py:413, v1/networks.py:717) — json_schema.py is not among them.
evidence.notes: Regex alphabet is disjoint ([^.[\]] excludes the iteration separator '.'), so no exponential backtracking; input is developer-controlled metadata.

findings.description: import_string() dynamically imports an arbitrary module/attribute from a caller-supplied dotted path — but this is the documented, opt-in purpose of the ImportString type, not an injectable sink
findings.reasoning: The taint source here is the `dotted_path` parameter of the private helper `_import_string_logic`, whose only in-library caller is `import_string(value)` in the same module (line 47). That function is wired into pydantic's `ImportString`/`PyObject` annotated type via `pydantic/types.py:461,465` (`core_schema.no_info_plain_validator_function(function=_validators.import_string, ...)`). Importing an object from a dotted string is the *documented and intended semantics* of that type — the docstring at lines 430-446 shows `Foo(call_date="datetime.date")` as the supported usage. There is no path in which pydantic itself feeds user input into this sink without the application developer explicitly annotating a model field as `ImportString`. Consequently the "vulnerability" is a deliberate design affordance, not an unvalidated sink: the library never decides on its own to import an attacker-supplied path. Exploitation would require the target application to declare an `ImportString` field populated from untrusted input, which is an application-level design choice (and even then `import_module`/`getattr` only resolve already-installed modules; no arbitrary code is executed unless the imported module's import side-effects are themselves malicious). The parsing is also defensive: colon count is bounded, empty module names rejected, and all failures converted into `ImportError`/`PydanticCustomError`. This matches the false-positive class of "library exposes a dynamic-import utility" rather than a reachable CWE-94 chains from request data.

findings.description: pydantic.v1.utils.import_string() dynamically imports a module from a caller-supplied dotted path — deliberate v1 PyObject/ImportString behaviour, not an injectable sink
findings.reasoning: The `dotted_path` parameter is consumed by `import_module(module_path)` at line 133. findings.description: Quadratic (polynomial) ReDoS in pydantic v1 pretty-email validation regex used by EmailStr/NameEmail validators
findings.code_snippet:
pretty_email_regex = re.compile(r'([\w ]*?) *<(.*)> *')
...
def validate_email(value: Union[str]) -> Tuple[str, str]:
    ...
    m = pretty_email_regex.fullmatch(value)
findings.reasoning: The regex `([\w ]*?) *<(.*)> *` contains two adjacent quantifiers that can match the same character class (`[\w ]` includes the literal space that the following ` *` also matches). Because the first group is lazy and the second quantifier is a greedy ` *`, the engine enumerates every split point: for an input of n spaces (or word chars/spaces) that does not contain `<`, the lazy group expands k = 0..n and, for every k, ` *` greedily consumes (n-k) characters and then backtracks one character at a time attempting to match `<`. This yields O(n^2) matching steps. `validate_email()` is invoked by the `EmailStr` and `NameEmail` validators on raw, fully attacker-controlled request values (JSON body / query params parsed into a pydantic v1 model), so a single large string of spaces produces a CPU-exhausting quadratic blowup — a classic polynomial ReDoS (CWE-1333). The call is `fullmatch`, so backtracking cannot terminate early at an anchor.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Attacker-controlled string -> BaseModel field typed EmailStr/NameEmail -> validators (str_validator, then cls.validate) -> validate_email(value) -> pretty_email_regex.fullmatch(value). No length limit or pre-screening is applied before the regex match.
evidence.notes: Overlapping character classes: `[\w ]*?` and ` *` both match spaces => quadratic backtracking. email-validator is only called AFTER the regex, so it cannot mitigate. Input of 100k spaces ~ 5e9 backtracking steps.

findings.description: User-controlled duration string is matched against ISO-8601 duration regex with unescaped dot and nested optional quantifiers, causing polynomial (super-linear) backtracking — parse_duration DoS
findings.reasoning: parse_duration() at line 234 matches arbitrary user input (any timedelta / Duration field value coming from JSON) against standard_duration_re and then iso8601_duration_re with no length limit. In iso8601_duration_re the `.` inside `(\d+(.\d+)?)` is unescaped (matches any character) and each sub-pattern is a nested `\d+` + optional `(.\d+)?`, so for an input such as "P" + "1"*N the engine has O(N^2) distinct ways to split the digits between `\d+` and `(.\d+)?` before failing on the missing 'D'/'H'/'M'/'S' terminator. This is reachable from any model field typed `timedelta` (Duration parsing) when a string is supplied, so an attacker can send a single large request body to burn CPU (CWE-1333 / CWE-407). It is not catastrophic exponential backtracking (bounded by quadratic), hence low severity but a real algorithmic-complexity DoS.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: User input (model field of type timedelta) -> parse_duration(value) -> standard_duration_re.match(value) or iso8601_duration_re.match(value). No length cap / timeout applied before regex evaluation.
evidence.notes: The unescaped '.' widens the sub-pattern to (any char)(\d+), multiplying the number of backtracking splits for long digit runs; failure at the terminating literal (D/H/M/S) forces the full quadratic search.

findings.description: standard_duration_re parses user-controlled timedelta strings with nested optional `\d+` groups; potential super-linear backtracking on crafted digit runs
findings.code_snippet:
standard_duration_re = re.compile(
    r'^'
    r'(?:(?P<days>-?\d+) (days?, )?)?'
    r'((?:(?P<hours>-?\d+):)(?=\d+:\d+))?'
    r'(?:(?P<minutes>-?\d+):)?'
    r'(?P<seconds>-?\d+)'
    r'(?:\.(?P<microseconds>\d{1,6})\d{0,6})?'
    r'$'
)
findings.reasoning: standard_duration_re is applied to the same untrusted `value` in parse_duration() and, unlike the ISO-8601 variant, all of its quantifiers are adjacent/optional over `\d+` (`(?:(?P<days>-?\d+) ...)?`, `(?:(?P<hours>-?\d+):)?`, `(?:(?P<minutes>-?\d+):)?`). Because the pattern is `^...$` anchored and the groups are optional, a digit-only payload can force the engine to repeatedly re-partition the same digits among the optional groups while the required literal separators (' ', ':', '.') fail. The blowup is at most polynomial and hard to trigger catastrophically because each optional group is terminated by a mandatory literal, so this needs manual verification/measurement of actual wall-clock growth rather than being a confirmed exploit.

findings.description: ReDoS via nested/overlapping quantifiers in v2 pretty-email regex (_build_pretty_email_regex), applied with fullmatch on attacker-controlled email strings
findings.code_snippet:
def _build_pretty_email_regex() -> re.Pattern:
    name_chars = r'[\w!#$%&\'*+\-/=?^_`{|}~]'
    unquoted_name_group = fr'((?:{name_chars}+\s+)*{name_chars}+)'
    quoted_name_group = r'"((?:[^"]|\")+)"'
    email_group = r'<\s*(.+)\s*>'
    return re.compile(rf'\s*(?:{unquoted_name_group}|{quoted_name_group})?\s*{email_group}\s*')


pretty_email_regex = _build_pretty_email_regex()

...
    m = pretty_email_regex.fullmatch(value)   # line 413, in validate_email(value: str)
findings.reasoning: pydantic/networks.py:389-397 is the v2 equivalent of the vulnerable v1 pretty_email_regex at pydantic/v1/networks.py:704 (which I confirmed as a true positive). The pattern builds `((?:name_chars+\s+)*name_chars+)` — a nested quantifier over overlapping character classes `[\w...]+` plus `\s+`, with the whole unquoted group optional and an optional alternative quoted group, then applied with `fullmatch()` to the raw user-supplied string in validate_email (line 413, reached by EmailStr / NameEmail validators). For a long input of word characters/spaces that ultimately fails to match (no trailing `<...>`), backtracking is proportional to the number of ways the string can be split across the inner repetition, producing catastrophic/exponential-with-degree behaviour (CWE-1333, CWE-407). Because EmailStr validation runs on request payloads, an attacker can submit a single long email-shaped string to pin a worker thread. Note: my primary confirmed instance is v1 (submitted separately); this v2 site was not listed in the query results but exhibits the same weakness, so it is reported as a newly discovered finding.
